title: Limitation is a Doorway to the Unbound Self
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing limitations and letting go of attachment and aversion in order to connect with a more unbound experience of life. This can be achieved by recognizing that our struggles and frustrations are not obstacles to overcome, but rather doorways to a deeper understanding of ourselves and the world around us. By surrendering our need for control and perfection, we can break open to new possibilities and find home and compassion in the present moment.

Thanks again, everybody.
I want to start with one of my favorite lines from the Genjokoan.
*The Buddha way is basically leaping clear of the many and the one.
Thus, there are birth and death, delusion and realization, sentient beings and Buddhas.
Yet, in attachment, blossoms fall and in aversion weeds spread.*
A little louder: *in attachment, blossoms fall and in aversion weeds spread.* Dogen is underscoring here the importance of no preference.
Can you guys hear me in the back?
Not come forward.
Come, come, come, come.
Norman talked quite a bit about preference in our June Samish sesshin.
How do we have no preference?
As Norman pointed out, we all have preference.
He said, you'd rather live than die, right?
So, is it possible to leap clear?
Many of our preferences are an expression of our will to survive, our survival instinct.
Recently our Kenyan adopted daughter came to visit.
She stayed for two weeks at our house with her four-month-old baby, who was just such an adorable little thing.
It had been a while since I'd hung out with babies, infants, and I noticed right away that he had very strong preferences.
He preferred to be full and satiated rather than having hunger pains.
He preferred a clean, fresh diaper to a dirty one.
He preferred being warm and cozy.
Right?
So we all prefer pleasant versus unpleasant experiences, right?
Well, I want to use this time together to tell you how I was given the opportunity to work with my own preferences that emerged during our recent Samish sesshin.
I've noticed repeatedly in myself, and again at sesshin, a strong preference for feeling spacious over feeling limited or contracted.
I often resist my own contractive reactions.

These different aspects of experience are referred to in many different ways in our tradition: the ultimate or historical perspective, big mind and little mind, emptiness or separateness, original self or conditioned self, enlightenment and delusion.
I asked myself, who wouldn't prefer boundlessness over separateness?
Yet, in attachment, blossoms fall and in aversion weeds spread.
I realized during sesshin that Dogen was pointing me toward an important lesson.

As many of you know, I was Co-Eno at the sesshin, and in that role I felt some responsibility for helping to create the container that holds sesshin, supporting the forms, the rituals, the schedule and the silence.
But in the first couple of days, I found myself engaged pretty continuously in conversation.
People were getting sick at sesshin, and the medical committee had an impromptu meeting to come up with a current COVID policy.
Somehow I found myself entwined in that process, which of course required a lot of speech.
Sesshin participants were also still adjusting to silence in the first days, so they would come up to me and ask, should I tell you or should I give you this note now?
It's an adjustment.
And for my first time, I had a wonderful Co-Eno, Desiree, so helpful.
But anytime you put two people together to share one job, there's a need to converse in order to coordinate efforts.
If I had been smart, I would have had a meeting before, or maybe on the very first day of sesshin, to coordinate these efforts and avoid the need to speak.
But alas, silly me, I didn't have that forethought.
So I found myself talking to my work buddy, my Co-Eno, who like me just wanted to do a good job.
With all that happening, in the first days of sesshin I felt frustrated with the situation, tense because my wish was to support silence, and critical of those talking around me, talking to me.
I felt the urge to control my environment.
Of course, I didn't like seeing and feeling these critical and controlling parts of myself.
I sat with myself.
I tried to avoid feeling critical and controlling.
My father, who was loving, had a critical and controlling edge, and I tried to convince myself I was not like him.
I didn't want to be like him.
I was making a great effort, in fact, to make those parts of myself go away.
So I tried working with a gatha.
I breathe in, I relax.
I breathe out, I let go.
You can guess: it did not work so well for me.
I thought at first that the gatha helped me to relax, but the following day my contention, my contraction, my efforts to control my environment came back with a fervor.
I went to dokusan and I shared with Norman that I was trying to let go, but trapped in the snares of my own mind.
First he mirrored that back to me: trapped in the snares of my own mind.
And I shared that my efforts to let go were actually counterproductive, because you can't actually effort to let go, right?
That's counterproductive.
So Norman's first reply was, have patience with yourself.
He's a kind man.
Have patience with yourself.
But then he said something that was quite pivotal for me in my process.
He pointed toward the bodhisattva heart that lives under the critic and the controller.
He helped me to see that love, a good-hearted intention, a bodhisattva spirit underlay the parts of myself that I was resisting.
What I most wanted, what was alive in my heart, was to support the depth of practice that can only be felt in the silence of sesshin.
Over the days of sesshin, I continued to think about this conversation with Norman.
And this verse from Dogen's Fukanzazengi kept coming up, echoing in my mind.
*The way is basically perfect and all-pervading.
How could it be contingent upon practice and realization?
The Dharma vehicle is free and untrammeled.
What need is there for concentrated effort?*
I was caught in the snares of my own mind, in my own efforts, my effort, ironically, to let go.
I was trying too hard.
Dogen goes on.
*Indeed, the whole body is far beyond the world's dust.
Who could believe in a means to brush it clean?
It is never apart from one right where one is.
It is never apart from one right where one is.*
From my conversation with Norman, I saw that even in the center of my bounded, constricted, limited self, it's a bodhisattva trying to express her heart.
And Dogen continues.
*If there is the slightest discrepancy, the way is as distant as heaven from earth.*
Well, a bodhisattva's heart expressed through the conditioned self is as distant as heaven from earth.
Yet it is never apart from one right where one is.
What we need is to look deeper.
Norman helped me to look deeper.
When I saw the vow of love under my efforts to control my environment, letting go naturally happened.
I relaxed, and I was able to accept the parts of myself that I was trying to push away, the critical and controlling parts.
I was able to accept those parts of my personality.
And when I did so, they softened, allowing me to connect with a more unbound experience.
Limitation is a doorway to the unbound self.
That's the name of this talk: limitation is a doorway to the unbound self.

Go deeper, right here.
Stand in the muddy water, right in the middle of your constricted self.

We all have one.

Yeah, it's very quiet.
Yeah.

Many of you know I teach Chinese medicine, and this is really at its core, so I was pretty happy to stumble upon this.
If you look at this symbol, it represents a very cyclic, dynamic relationship in which the yang becomes yin, becomes yang, becomes yin.
Right at the center of the biggest yang you find yin, right in its heart.
And in the heart of the biggest yin, you find yang.
In the center of what Okumura calls the limited individual self is Buddha's heart.
In the center of my critical and controlling self, I found my bodhisattva heart, my wish to help and support the sangha.
In my dokusan with Chris today, she used the metaphor of a swinging gate.
On both sides of the gate we have endarkenment, enlightenment, absolute, relative, limited self, boundless self: the swinging gate.
I hope it's okay for me to quote you, Talus.

Another metaphor that really, I think, works in talking about this.
So, yeah, we have some time.

Maybe it's a relationship to work.
Maybe it's a relationship with a family member, a friend, or maybe someone here in our sangha.

What is the quality of the contraction that you feel?
In what ways do you feel small or limited here?
Do you experience yourself as separate or bounded?
How does the contraction or constriction feel in your body?
How is it expressed in this relationship or situation?
And then I'm going to invite us into triads.
In your triad, you'll each get a chance to speak.
You could briefly describe the way you feel, or the feeling of contraction, in that relationship.
But it's fine to keep it brief.

What might be living in your bodhisattva heart?
What good intention might be underlying that contracted place?
Just see what comes up.
There's no right or wrong answer, and you may or may not find a contracted place.
You may or may not find what your intention is under it.
But it's just an opportunity to explore and see what comes up.
There are a couple of people here I don't recognize, so maybe you haven't done triads before.
I'll explain.
We'll get into groups of three and each person will have five minutes to talk.
Okay, four.
I was deliberating between four and five.
Four minutes to talk, and just explore and see what comes up.
You can allow it to be just a stream of consciousness sharing.
What comes up for you may not have anything to do with what I ask.
But again, I'll reiterate: describe the feeling or the contraction that might be alive in this relationship.
You can keep it brief.
Your listeners don't need to understand the details.
It's more important to share with the group what your deeper desire is, what's in your bodhisattva heart, what good intentions might be underlying this in you.
So you'll have four minutes to talk.

So it's actually great to sit together in the silence.
I know sometimes people are like, I'm done, go on to the next person.
